scopeReview: SPS-2.C.1–2: causes and political/social/economic consequences of population aging. Explicit age conventions, count/share distinction, component dependency, labor participation, pensions, care and access. No stereotypes or real-world financial/medical advice.
varietyReview: Two tables, paired-age bars and a proportional count map; additional weighted mortality and funding calculations independently checked. Concepts address causes, environment, policy limits, politics and unpaid care. All five skills, varied keys and foundational/intermediate/challenging items.
repetitionReview: Unlike2.3 shape/share identification, these tasks examine aging with a constant older count, unchanged total dependency hiding rising old-age dependency, and contributors distinct from potential support. Map reverses count/share ranking for service planning; no numeric-only clone of an earlier pyramid question.
referenceNote: Official curriculum and institutional ageing context checked; UN page search excerpt available but direct fetch unavailable, so no claim of full-page review. Original synthetic data/calculations and conditional mechanisms; no third-party catalog additions or human review claim.

questions.correctOption: The share aged 65+ rose from 10% to 12.5% even though its count stayed at 1,000.
questions.independentReview: Summed earlier2000+7000+1000=10000 and later1000+6000+1000=8000; computed1000/10000=.10 and1000/8000=.125. Count change0 but share change+2.5 percentage points.

questions.correctOption: Total age dependency stays the same while old-age dependency rises.
questions.independentReview: Recomputed dependency totals(2500+1500)/6000=(1600+2400)/6000=2/3 and older ratios1500/6000=.25,2400/6000=.4. Age-based ratios do not identify actual employment or individual dependence.

questions.correctOption: Rural has a larger older share, but City has a larger older count.
questions.independentReview: Computed250/1000=.25 and1500/10000=.15, while1500/250=6. Symbol areas encode counts with a6:1 area ratio; they do not encode age percentages or prove identical needs.

questions.correctOption: Equal age ratios can conceal different numbers of contributors per older resident.
questions.independentReview: Independently calculated age support6000/2000=3 each and contributor ratios3000/2000=1.5,5000/2000=2.5. Kept potential demographic support distinct from actual contributions and from solvency.

questions.correctOption: Persistently lower fertility combined with more people surviving into older ages.
questions.independentReview: Checked numerator/denominator mechanisms separately: fewer young entrants and more survival to old age can increase older share. This concerns population composition, not the claim that an individual’s biological aging is caused by fertility decline.

questions.correctOption: More residents are in older age groups with higher death rates, changing the weighted average.
questions.independentReview: Verified with a separate example: young/older rates2/20 per1000 give3.8 with10% older and7.4 with30% older. Rates unchanged, weights changed. No medical-care decline can be inferred from this crude comparison alone.

questions.correctOption: Improve step-free routes, crossing times and access to essential destinations.
questions.independentReview: Mapped the stated mobility/access goal to physical routes and destinations. Verified against age-friendly-environment principles without treating all older people as disabled, inactive or in need of institutions.

Independently multiplied recipients by1000 and divided by5000, obtaining400/500; checked total receipts exactly match2million/2.5million. Assumptions exclude assets, other revenue and contribution differences.

questions.correctOption: Age rules can change potential participation, but health, job availability and unequal work conditions affect actual outcomes.
questions.independentReview: Separated legal eligibility, actual labor participation and chronological composition. Conditional effects avoid asserting a policy recommendation or universal capacity to extend working lives.

questions.correctOption: All older voters share the same party preference and will vote as one bloc.
questions.independentReview: Distinguished the given aggregate share from unobserved within-group preferences. A larger older electorate permits investigation of political consequences but cannot establish unanimous party choice or turnout.

questions.correctOption: Examine care needs, unpaid hours, lost earnings and how responsibilities are distributed.
questions.independentReview: Traced household care demands to labor-market and distributional consequences rather than only government expenditures. Avoided equating every older person with dependence or assuming that constrained work choices reveal preferences.
